summary: Paul leaves Athens for Corinth and works with Aquila and Priscilla, Jewish artisans recently expelled from Rome under Claudius. He reasons in the synagogue, then focuses on Gentile mission after resistance, while Crispus the synagogue ruler and many Corinthians believe. A night vision promises the Lord's presence and a numerous people, so Paul remains eighteen months. Opponents bring him before Gallio, but the proconsul treats the dispute as an internal matter of words, names, and Jewish law. Paul later sails with Priscilla and Aquila, briefly visits Ephesus, completes the journey, and begins another. In Ephesus the eloquent Alexandrian Apollos teaches accurately but incompletely until Priscilla and Aquila privately explain God's way more precisely.
whyItMatters: Mission is sustained by work, partnership, hospitality, correction, legal space, and divine encouragement—not Paul acting alone. The chapter gives unusual visibility to Priscilla and Aquila as coworkers who host, travel, teach, and protect another teacher's dignity. It also provides one of Acts' strongest chronological anchors through Gallio while showing Roman nonintervention as pragmatic rather than theological endorsement.

context.author: The Luke–Acts narrator concluding the second mission and beginning the third
context.audience: Readers watching durable communities form through coworkers, labor, teaching, and public law
context.date: Paul's Corinth stay overlaps Gallio's proconsulship around AD 51–52
context.setting: Corinth, Cenchreae, Ephesus, Caesarea, Antioch, Galatia, Phrygia, and Achaia
context.literaryForm: Travel and ministry summary with legal hearing, vow notice, and Apollos correction scene

outline.heading: Paul works and witnesses with Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth
Gallio dismisses the synagogue opponents' case
Paul travels onward while Priscilla and Aquila teach Apollos

keyVerses.text: The Lord said to Paul in the night by a vision, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent;
keyVerses.why: Divine encouragement meets fear and commands continued public witness.

keyVerses.text: He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.
keyVerses.why: Mature coworkers correct an able teacher privately, precisely, and constructively.

keyVerses.text: for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.
keyVerses.why: Apollos's received instruction strengthens his public scriptural case, though the local polemic needs careful qualification.

questions.question: What trade did Paul, Aquila, and Priscilla share?
questions.answer: Skēnopoios literally suggests tentmaker, but it can include broader leatherworking or woven shelter work. Ancient artisans often lived and worked in household shops, making the couple's trade both economic support and relational mission space. Paul reasons on Sabbaths and works with his hands rather than treating labor as unrelated to ministry.

questions.question: What was Claudius's expulsion of Jews from Rome?
questions.answer: Roman writers report that Emperor Claudius expelled or restricted Jews around AD 49 after disturbances associated, in Suetonius's wording, with ‘Chrestus,’ possibly disputes about Christ. Acts simply says all Jews were ordered to leave Rome, explaining why Aquila and Priscilla recently arrived. The measure reveals the insecurity of Jewish life under imperial power.

questions.question: Does ‘your blood be on your own heads’ mean Paul permanently abandons Jews?
questions.answer: The phrase is prophetic responsibility language addressed to resistant hearers in one synagogue. Paul moves next door, the synagogue ruler Crispus believes, and Paul will enter synagogues in subsequent cities. ‘From now on I will go to the Gentiles’ describes a local mission turn and dominant trajectory, not an oath never again to speak with Jews.

questions.question: Why does the Lord tell Paul not to fear?
questions.answer: The command implies fear is real amid opposition; courage is not evidence that Paul never feels threatened. The promise ‘I am with you’ echoes prophetic call narratives, and ‘I have many people in this city’ anticipates a community not yet fully visible. Paul responds by remaining eighteen months to teach rather than expecting instant protection without sustained work.

questions.question: Why is Gallio so important for dating Acts?
questions.answer: An inscription from Delphi helps date Lucius Junius Gallio's proconsulship in Achaia to roughly AD 51–52. Because Paul appears before him during an eighteen-month Corinthian stay, the hearing anchors a portion of Paul's chronology. Gallio's title also fits Corinth's status as provincial capital.

questions.question: Does Gallio declare Christianity legally protected?
questions.answer: He refuses to judge what he sees as a dispute about words, names, and Jewish law because no crime or vicious act is alleged. That dismissal creates immediate space for Paul but is not a general imperial ruling or endorsement of the gospel. His indifference to Sosthenes's beating also makes him a poor model of justice.

questions.question: What vow did Paul complete by cutting his hair?
questions.answer: The brief notice resembles a Nazirite vow, in which hair is grown and later cut, but Acts does not state the vow's purpose or every procedure; the location Cenchreae also raises questions because completion offerings belonged in Jerusalem. The detail shows continued Jewish devotional practice without giving enough information for certainty.

questions.question: What did Apollos know—and lack?
questions.answer: He is eloquent, powerful in the Scriptures, instructed in ‘the way of the Lord,’ fervent, and accurate about Jesus, yet knows only John's baptism. That unusual combination may reflect an incomplete stage of the message rather than false teaching. Priscilla and Aquila explain the way more accurately without public humiliation, and Apollos receives the correction fruitfully.

questions.question: Why is Priscilla sometimes named before Aquila?
questions.answer: Acts names Aquila first when introducing the married pair but Priscilla first in ministry contexts here, as Paul also sometimes does in letters. The order may signal her prominence, status, or teaching role, though Luke does not explain it. Together they demonstrate that a woman participates directly in the theological formation of a renowned male teacher.

glossary.def: Tentmaker or related leather/textile artisan; the precise ancient trade range is debated.
Governor of a senatorial Roman province; Gallio held this office in Achaia.
An Alexandrian Jewish Scripture teacher who becomes an influential coworker after receiving fuller instruction.
